newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Rebels for hostages swap under way - Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: Rebels for hostages swap under way - Tajikistan.

text.p: The Tajik government began a late-night rebels-for-hostages swap on Friday, but the outcome was unclear as the deal depended on the goodwill of the rebel Islamic group holding 14 foreign and Russian hostages.
Officials said rebel leader Bakhram Sadirov had allowed three hostages to leave the captors' mountain-top base some 80 km (50 miles) from the capital Dushanbe.
They were expected to return with a Russian diplomat and a group of rebels flown in by Tajik authorities for the exchange.
After the arriving rebels had been united with their comrades, all 14 hostages were due to be freed.
"He (Sadirov) is in a very agitated state," Russian Deputy Prime Minister Vitaly Ignatenko said on Russian television. "His demands are becoming more severe...but we have met them all."
The hostages include three U.N. observers -- two from Switzerland and one from Ukraine -- four Russian journalists and four workers with the U.N. refugee agency.

Tajikistan's security minister was also seized last weekend when he tried to negotiate with the hostage-takers, who once backed the former Soviet republic's Islamic opposition but whose loyalties are now unclear.

The swap deal agreed to by the Tajik government apparently leaves open the risk that Sadirov could keep the hostages as well as the Russian diplomat overseeing the exchange after the additional rebels arrived.
Russian television quoted the diplomat, Gennady Sizov, as saying the situation around the base was "very tense".
Adding to the drama was uncertainty about the fate of one of the U.N. observers. Sadirov said on Thursday he had killed an observer, but on Friday he told Ignatenko that the report was untrue.
The hostage crisis has highlighted the instability of Tajikistan, an impoverished former Soviet republic bordering Afghanistan and China.

President Boris Yeltsin and other top leaders in Russia, whose soldiers help police the border with Afghanistan, have expressed concern about the hostage situation and called for a peaceful resolution.
Armed groups opposed to Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov are scattered across the country and some fighters, such as those loyal to Sadirov and his brother Rivzon, are based in Afghanistan.
Tajik government spokesman Zafar Saidov said the rebels had threatened to take their captives to the mountains and launch a guerrilla war unless their demands were met.
